hints: Walk through text one character at a time. When you see a character that equals some letter of word, it can extend every partial copy that was waiting for exactly that letter.
Counting DP: dp[j] = number of ways to pick word[0..j-1] from the part of text seen so far. Each text character adds to the entries it can extend; use 64-bit counts.

1. dp[0] = 1 (the empty prefix can be picked in one way), the rest 0.
  2. For each character c of text:
  3. go j from word.length down to 1; if word[j-1] == c, do dp[j] += dp[j-1].
  4. Going right-to-left makes sure one text character is used at most once per copy.
  5. Return dp[word.length].

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try every set of positions in text of size word.length and check which spell word.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Same recurrence on a single 1D array, updated from right to left.

explain: For text = "aabb", word = "ab": after the two as, dp[1] = 2 (two ways to pick "a"). The first b adds dp[1] to dp[2] → 2, and the second b adds 2 more → 4. The invariant is that after each text character, dp[j] counts exactly the ways using only characters seen so far. Edge cases: an empty word gives 1, and a word longer than text naturally ends at 0; use long because counts grow fast.
recognize: 'In how many ways can word be picked out of text as a subsequence' → counting DP over prefixes (distinct subsequences).
